description: Independent research and development with satellite fire observations.
summary:
Brasa Orbit puts two NASA active-fire records, MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP, side by side in one day × month × year calendar for an area of interest. The sensors observe the same ground with different pixel sizes, overpass times and numbers of satellites, so their detection counts are not interchangeable: a change of sensor can look like a change on the ground. Using NASA FIRMS standard yearly files for Brazil (2018–2020), the calendar shows daily counts for central-eastern Mato Grosso and part of MATOPIBA, with a monthly VIIRS/MODIS ratio labelled as a naive diagnostic, not a harmonization. Both sensors agree on timing: September is the peak month every year in both regions. In central-eastern Mato Grosso, VIIRS records 3.2–3.6× as many detections as MODIS over a full year, yet in 9 months (February–April of 2018, 2019 and 2020) MODIS records clearly more, an unexpected inversion still to be verified. In these data, no single scaling factor fits every month. This is a first step toward harmonization: measuring the seasonal gap any harmonization must correct. The next step is a rate per observed area that separates fire activity from observation coverage.
A new Unusual Months panel compares each sensor with its own same-month record, flags months reaching 1.5x their usual level, and shows whether MODIS and VIIRS agree; with only three years of baseline, it is an exploratory screen, not a harmonized product.
details:
What it does. Brasa Orbit is a web calendar of satellite fire detections. For an area of interest, it shows daily MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP detection counts side by side for 2018–2020, browsable by day, month and year. A region selector switches between central-eastern Mato Grosso (lon −56 to −52, lat −17 to −10) and part of MATOPIBA, the Cerrado agricultural frontier (lon −47 to −43, lat −12 to −5), in Brazil. MODIS counts include both Terra and Aqua; VIIRS here is Suomi NPP only. A monthly VIIRS/MODIS ratio panel shows where the two records agree and where they diverge.

How it works. A Python script reads the NASA FIRMS standard yearly country files for Brazil (MODIS version 6.03 and VIIRS S-NPP version 2, as labelled in the files). It keeps detections with type = 0 (presumed vegetation fire), day and night, assigns dates in UTC, clips each region with half-open boxes and counts detections per day. The result is a small JSON file that records the SHA-256 checksum of every input file. A static web page in HTML, CSS and JavaScript renders the calendar, the ratio panel and a table. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and needs no login.

Tools and languages. Python 3 (standard library only), HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no external libraries, Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages.

Benefits. Early-warning professionals, scientists and land managers can see where the two records agree and where they differ before comparing periods, and avoid reading a change of sensor as a change on the ground.

Creativity. MODIS and VIIRS appear in the same calendar for one area of interest, and the limits stay on screen: pixels of about 1 km versus 375 m, a detection is not a fire and not burned area, and "no detection recorded" is not "no fire". It shows both records for the same area and days, as a first step toward harmonization: measuring the seasonal gap any harmonization must correct. Both sensors agree on timing (September peak every year, in both regions), while the February–April inversion is unexpected and still to be verified. The next step is a rate per observed area, Y = 1000 · ΣD / E, where E is the usable area both sensors observed on comparable overpasses. It separates an observed zero from a missing rate.

Unusual months. Each sensor is compared with its own record: a month's index is its count divided by the mean of that month in the other two years, so a stable sensitivity gap (VIIRS sees ~3–4x more) drops out. Months at 1.5x or above in both sensors read "unusual in both sensors"; in one only, "sensors disagree". Central-eastern Mato Grosso, Aug–Nov 2020: MODIS 1.8–3.4x, VIIRS 1.9–4.5x. Exploratory (three-year baseline).

Limits. The calendar is not harmonized: it shows raw counts, and the ratio is a naive diagnostic. FIRMS files carry no cloud-cover or missing-data information. The scope is two regions in Brazil, 2018–2020. Suomi NPP stopped producing new observations on 2 Nov 2026. The project makes no causal claims and is not an operational alert, a forecast or a burned-area product.
